root.name: Philidor Defense: Steinitz Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. Bc4 Be7 4. c3

overview: White develops Bc4 and plays c3 to prepare d4, while Black holds e5 with ...d6 and ...Be7 and aims for ...Nf6, ...O-O and a compact set-up. White usually gets more space after d4, and Black must free his game with ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right time. The game is quiet, with few forcing lines.

white_ideas.idea: Build the centre with c3 and d4
Develop smoothly with Nbd2, O-O and Re1 and use the space

black_ideas.idea: Hold e5 with Nd7 or Nf6 and castle
Break with ...exd4 or ...d5 to free the game

typical_structures.structure: White d4/e4 centre against Black d6/e5 chain, often resolved by ...exd4 cxd4
Hanham-style Black set-up with pawns on d6 and e5

character.notes: A cramped but resilient set-up for Black with little early risk.

soundness.notes: Sound; the Philidor is dynamically balanced.

structure.notes: Flexible until White plays d4 and Black decides how to resolve the centre.

approach.notes: A respectable but less common defence; standard rather than offbeat.

level.notes: Clear plans and few traps beyond move-order care.

character.reason: Black builds a compact, hard-to-break set-up.

soundness.reason: The Philidor is considered sound if passive.

structure.reason: The centre stays undecided until d4 and ...exd4 or ...d5.

approach.reason: Less common but respectable at every level.

level.reason: Plans are clear but Black must time the freeing break.

plans.reason: White gains space while Black waits to free the game.
